The same openness enables deliberate falsification, selective exposure, ideological polarization, declining news diversity, and poorer-quality political information, all of which weaken citizens’ ability to make informed decisions. Survey evidence captures this duality: across 19 countries, a median of 73% thought connectivity had made people better informed about current events, but 84% thought it had made people easier to manipulate with false information, while 65% believed political opinions had become more divided. The democratic balance is therefore negative because participation is valuable only when citizens can share a reasonably reliable informational environment, whereas misinformation and polarization directly undermine the deliberation that participation is meant to improve. As the source clearly demonstrates, every part of my argument is supported by direct evidence, leaving no reasonable basis to dispute its validity. 10. The response explicitly integrates and references the domain specific analyses (positive and negative findings) when weighing the overall beneficial or detrimental effects of social media.
